person: Hana Kowalczyk is a 34-year-old who runs a one-person shop selling ceramics and linen goods from a studio behind her house in Oregon, on her own site plus two marketplaces. In the busy season she has ten card disputes open at once, mostly on forty-dollar orders, and she cannot keep the reason codes straight. A 'chargeback protection' app once sent the same template to every dispute and lost most of them, so she is wary. She wants to know quickly whether this is meant for a shop her size and what Athena needs from her, because she has orders to pack.
stated_up_front: Hi! I've got ten chargebacks open and honestly I can't tell which ones are worth fighting. Can you go through them and fight the ones I can win, and tell me which to just let go? Is this even meant for a tiny shop like mine?

facts.about: How many disputes are open and typical size
facts.truth: Ten open, mostly around $40 each, the biggest is a $186 set of dinner plates.

facts.about: A dispute she thinks is fair to fight (delivered)
facts.truth: A $64 linen table runner order shipped via USPS and shows delivered on 2 October 2026 to the full address in Portland, with a signature-free drop at the door.
A $52 mug set order from 12 September 2026 was never shipped because a kiln batch cracked, and she never got round to telling the customer.

facts.about: A refund she promised but never paid
facts.truth: She told a customer in Postwren on 28 September 2026 that she would refund $38 for a chipped bowl but forgot to issue it.

facts.about: A repeat customer on a fraud dispute
facts.truth: One customer, who she knows as 'Dana R.', bought three times since the spring from the same address and phone, then disputed the latest $45 order as not recognised.

facts.about: A fraud dispute with just one earlier order
facts.truth: A $71 order disputed as fraud where the same card bought once before in July 2026 from a different phone.
She refunded $29 for a late coaster set on 6 October 2026 and the customer still disputed it.
About 60% on her own site, the rest on two marketplaces, and the disputes on her own site are the ones she has to answer herself.
She packs orders in the mornings and can only look at this in the evening, after about 7pm Pacific.
The protection app she paid $29 a month for lost seven of her last ten disputes, so she cancelled it in August 2026.

unknowns: Which reason code each dispute carries or what it means
The processor's due date for each dispute, or the difference between the two dates shown
What counts as enough proof for a fraud dispute, such as matching device or IP on earlier orders
Whether the customer's IP address or device matched on the earlier orders
